title: How to Give Feedback, and How to Take It
summary: Feedback runs both ways. The SBI model, when feedback makes work worse, how to make praise useful, and how to hear hard notes without getting defensive.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's Thursday. For two weeks you've noticed that a teammate's PRs land with no tests for the error paths. Every time you start typing a comment about it, you delete it. Meanwhile your lead left two words on your design doc this morning, "Not convinced.", and you've been replaying them since lunch.

That's one skill seen from both sides. Giving feedback means saying the useful thing so the other person can act on it. Receiving feedback means hearing it without getting knocked off balance. Nobody teaches either one in a CS degree, yet both decide how fast you and your team improve. This post covers both: what useful feedback looks like, a simple structure for it, phrasing you can borrow, and what to do when the note is about you.

Why it feels risky on both sides

The giver worries about conflict. What if they push back, what if it gets awkward, what if I'm wrong? Saying nothing feels safer this week. The receiver worries about looking bad. When you're new, junior or still proving yourself, a critical comment can feel like proof of the thing you already fear about yourself.

So both people stay polite and nothing changes. The teammate keeps shipping PRs without error-path tests. You keep wondering what "not convinced" meant. The problem doesn't go away. It just grows until someone has to deal with it under deadline pressure.

The cost of silence

When Google studied what made its teams effective, psychological safety came first of the five dynamics it found, ahead of dependability, structure and clarity, meaning and impact. Google's write-up borrows Amy Edmondson's definition: a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. On those teams, people trust that nobody will embarrass or punish them for admitting a mistake (Google re:Work, Understand team effectiveness). Every piece of feedback, given or taken, adds to that belief or chips away at it.

The good part: giving and taking feedback are skills. You get better with practice, and small changes in wording make a real difference.

What useful feedback has in common

Useful feedback tends to share four traits:

  • Specific. It names a file, a function, a sentence in a doc, a moment in a meeting. "This service does too much" is a start. "UserService handles both login and profile updates, so you can't test either one alone" is something the author can fix.
  • Timely. A review comment lands best while the author still remembers why they wrote the code. A note about a meeting lands best that same week, while both of you remember the meeting.
  • About the work. "You always overcomplicate things" puts a person on trial. "In this PR the mapping logic is split across three layers, and I got lost following it" gives them something to look at.
  • Points forward. "Hard to read" leaves people stuck. "Pulling the mapping into a named function would make this easier to follow" gives them a first step.

There's solid research behind the third trait. In 1996 Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi pooled 607 effect sizes from feedback studies. On average, feedback improved performance. Yet more than a third of the feedback interventions made performance worse. Their explanation: feedback helps less as it pulls the person's attention away from the task and toward themselves (Kluger and DeNisi, Psychological Bulletin, 1996). That's a good reason to keep a comment on the code, the doc or the meeting, and off the person.

A simple structure: Situation, Behavior, Impact

The Center for Creative Leadership teaches a three-part shape called Situation-Behavior-Impact, or SBI (CCL). Name the specific situation. Describe the behavior someone could have seen or heard, with no judgment attached. Then say what it caused. CCL also suggests a fourth step: ask about intent, with something like "What were you hoping to accomplish?" That turns a one-way message into a conversation.

Here's how it sounds out loud: "In yesterday's incident review, you cut in three times while the on-call engineer was walking through the timeline. The rest of us lost the thread, and she stopped talking after the third time. What was going on for you there?"

No guesses about motives ("you wanted to take over the room"), no labels ("you're dismissive"), no "always". Just what happened and what it caused, plus room for the other side. Maybe they spotted a wrong timestamp and panicked. Now you can talk about that.

From first reaction to a useful comment

Most of us feel that something is off before we can say why. The work is turning that feeling into a sentence the other person can use. A few common pairs:

What you feel like sayingWhat helps more
"This is too complicated." "parseConfig reads env vars, validates the schema and fills in defaults. Splitting those three would make each one easy to test." Names the exact problem and a fix.
"I don't like this approach." "I'm worried that polling every 500 ms will load the database at our current traffic. Did you consider a webhook or a queue?" Ties the worry to a concrete risk and asks.
"You always miss the edge cases." "processItems throws a TypeError on an empty array, around line 42. Can we add a guard or a test?" Drops "always" and sticks to this PR.
"This needs a rewrite." "Data fetching and rendering are tangled in this component, so changing one means touching both. Could we pull the fetching into a custom hook before merging?" Names the structural issue and one first step.
"I disagree." "My concern is that this ties us to a sync interface, which could block the event loop under load. What trade-offs did you weigh?" States the concern and invites their reasoning.
"Good job." (and nothing else) "The error boundary in DataTable catches both network and parsing errors without leaking details up the tree. I'm copying that pattern." Tells them what to keep doing.
Read it as the author

Before you send a comment, read it as the person who'll get it. Do they know exactly what to change, and why? If either answer is "not really", add one sentence. That one sentence is usually the difference between a confusing comment and a useful one.

Praise counts as feedback too

Engineers tend to find pointing out problems easier than pointing out what works. Specific praise tells someone what to keep doing, and that's as useful as hearing what to stop.

The catch is vague praise. "Great work on the migration" is nice and teaches nothing. What was great? The rollback plan? The status updates to the product team? Running it on a canary before touching production? Each of those is a different lesson. Name it and the person can repeat it on purpose.

  • Use the same SBI shape: "In Wednesday's incident review, you walked through the failure step by step, and the whole room got the root cause in five minutes."
  • Say what it made possible: "Because your rollback plan was written down, the on-call engineer knew exactly what to do at 2 a.m."
  • Say it in public when it's earned. A shout-out in the team channel or a retro shows everyone what good looks like here, and it means a lot to someone new.
  • Say it soon. Praise loses value with time, same as criticism.

The same applies inside PRs. A review with only critical comments starts to feel like a minefield, even when every comment is fair. One line of specific praise takes ten seconds and changes how the rest reads. There's more on that in How to Review Code Kindly.

Taking feedback without bristling

Receiving is often harder than giving. The note arrives while you still care a lot about the work. Sometimes it's badly worded. And the line between "they don't like my code" and "they don't like me" feels thin in the moment.

Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen, who wrote Thanks for the Feedback, describe three triggers that make people push feedback away (Program on Negotiation, Harvard Law School):

  • Truth triggers: the content seems wrong or unfair, so you start arguing with it.
  • Relationship triggers: your reaction is really about who said it.
  • Identity triggers: the note hits how you see yourself, and some people feel that hit harder than others.

Naming which one fired already helps. Then a few habits:

  1. Pause before you reply. A spike of defensiveness means the note touched something. Reread it in ten minutes. In person, "Let me think about that" is a complete answer.
  2. Ask where it comes from and where it's headed. "What did you see that made you think that?" and "What would you do differently?" turn a vague note like "this feels overengineered" into something you can work with.
  3. Separate the message from the delivery. Someone can be clumsy and right at the same time. You don't have to reward the clumsy part to keep the right part.
  4. Say thanks and decide later. "Thanks for flagging this, I'll think it over" is honest and doesn't commit you to agreeing.
  5. Ask before it's offered. Stone and Heen suggest a narrow question: "What's one thing I could do better?" Asking for one thing gets you something concrete.
On disagreeing

Taking feedback well doesn't mean accepting all of it. You can disagree, with reasons: "I see the concern. I went this way because the API pages at 50 items. Does that change things?" What hurts is going silent and ignoring the note. The person who gave it learns that speaking up wasn't worth the effort.

Feedback to peers and to your manager

Most advice assumes a senior talking to a junior. Two other directions matter just as much and get far less attention.

To a peer

Telling a teammate at your level something honest feels awkward because there's no title to lean on. Do it anyway. A few things help: start with a question when you're not sure ("I noticed X, was that on purpose?"), say it one-on-one before it ever comes up in a group, and keep it on the work. Over months, the teammate who tells you the truth becomes the one you trust most. People who only say what you want to hear are pleasant company and not much help.

To your manager

Feedback upward is harder, because there's a power gap and no amount of team spirit erases it. What works:

  • Use your 1:1. Feedback about your manager's behavior doesn't belong in a team meeting. It puts them on the spot in front of an audience.
  • Talk about the effect on your work. "When sprint scope changes in the last two days, I struggle to prioritize. Could we lock it a bit earlier?" is easier to hear than "You keep changing scope at the last minute."
  • Bring one or two recent examples, plus what would help. A pile of complaints saved up over months is hard for anyone to act on.
  • Pick the moment. Not during an outage, and not five minutes before their own big meeting.

Where feedback happens

The same habits apply everywhere, but each setting has its own rules.

In code review

Written comments are async, permanent and read without your tone of voice. "This is a bit long" sounds fine across a desk and cold in a PR. Add the reason and a direction: "This is a bit long. Pulling the validation into its own function would make it easier to scan." The full playbook, with comment labels and PR size data, is in How to Review Code Kindly.

In 1:1s

A 1:1 is the right place for anything personal, sensitive or about patterns over time: career direction, how someone handles conflict, a habit you've noticed for a month. It's live and private, so you can see how the note lands and adjust. Bring one or two specific points, never a list saved up since last quarter. There's a whole post on running a good 1:1 if you want more on the meeting itself.

In incident reviews

Incident reviews have one firm rule: blameless. Google's SRE book puts it this way: a blameless postmortem focuses on the contributing causes "without indicting any individual or team", and assumes everyone involved had good intentions. Its reasoning is short: "You can't 'fix' people, but you can fix systems and processes" (Site Reliability Engineering, Postmortem Culture). So the feedback goes to alerts, runbooks and tooling. "Our alerting missed the memory leak for six hours. Should we add a threshold alert?" fits. "Why didn't you catch this?" doesn't.

As the team grows

Small teams usually run on informal feedback: a word after standup, a thread in Slack, a chat over lunch. That's fast and frequent, which is great. The risk is that it's uneven, so some people hear a lot and others hear nothing. As a team grows, a bit of structure keeps it fair: regular 1:1s, real retro time, written review norms. Then feedback reaches everyone, including the people who don't happen to eat lunch with the lead.

Try this week

  • Pick one piece of feedback you've been sitting on and write it in SBI form. End it with a question about intent.
  • In your next review, leave one comment of specific praise next to your critiques.
  • Ask one person "What's one thing I could do better?" and only say thanks in reply.
  • Next time a note stings, name the trigger (truth, relationship or identity) before you answer.
  • If you lead a team, check who hasn't heard any feedback from you this month.

Some feedback is harder than a PR comment, like telling someone their behavior is hurting the team. For that one, there's a separate post on preparing for difficult feedback. And if you want to help someone grow over months, keep going with Mentoring Engineers.

faqs.q: How do I give constructive feedback to a coworker without hurting the relationship?
faqs.a: Keep it on the work. Name the situation, describe what you saw or heard without guessing at motives, and say what it caused. That's the Situation-Behavior-Impact (SBI) model from the Center for Creative Leadership. Skip words like "always", say it privately first, and finish by asking what they were trying to do. Specific, honest feedback given this way tends to build trust over time.

faqs.q: What is the SBI feedback model?
faqs.a: SBI stands for Situation, Behavior, Impact, a structure taught by the Center for Creative Leadership. You name the specific situation ("in yesterday's incident review"), describe the observable behavior ("you cut in three times while the on-call engineer was talking"), then state the impact ("we lost the thread and she stopped talking"). CCL also suggests a fourth step: ask about intent, for example "What were you hoping to accomplish?"

Yes. A 1996 meta-analysis by Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi pooled 607 effect sizes and found that feedback improved performance on average, yet more than a third of feedback interventions decreased it. Their explanation is that feedback helps less as it pulls attention away from the task and toward the person's sense of self. That's a strong argument for keeping feedback about the work.

faqs.q: How do I take critical feedback without getting defensive?
faqs.a: Notice what set you off. Douglas Stone and Sheila Heen describe three triggers: the content seems wrong (truth), your reaction is about who said it (relationship), or it hits how you see yourself (identity). Pause before replying, ask what they observed and what they'd suggest, separate the message from the delivery, and say thanks before you decide what to do with it.

faqs.q: How do I give feedback to my manager?
faqs.a: Use your 1:1, never a group meeting. Describe the effect on your work instead of judging their character, for example: "When sprint scope changes in the last two days, I struggle to prioritize. Could we lock it earlier?" Bring one or two recent examples and say what would help. Pick a moment when they're not in the middle of an outage or about to walk into a big meeting.
